definition: Deliberately bland and inoffensive, so that it upsets no one but also excites no one.
example: The hotel lobby was painted an anodyne beige that no guest would ever remember.
nuance: Unlike innocuous, which simply means harmless, anodyne suggests a dull blandness that is often chosen on purpose to avoid any reaction.
prompt: A company spokesperson must answer reporters' questions about a delayed product launch.
options: The spokesperson gave an anodyne statement that promised nothing and offended no one.
The spokesperson's anodyne remarks were so inflammatory that reporters gasped in shock.
The statement was anodyne, so no reporter could figure out who had written it.
An anodyne crowd of reporters shouted angry questions over one another.
reasons: A safe, empty statement designed to avoid any controversy fits the word exactly.
Inflammatory remarks provoke strong reactions, the reverse of what this word describes.
This confuses the word with anonymous; it describes bland content, not hidden authorship.
A loud, agitated crowd is the opposite of mild and unprovoking.

practice.prompt: A teenager is choosing a song to play during dinner with picky relatives.
options: She chose an anodyne pop ballad, figuring no one at the table could object to it.
She chose an anodyne punk anthem packed with shocking lyrics meant to rattle her stern uncles.
She picked an anodyne recording from the 1920s simply because it was the oldest one she owned.
Her grandmother found the anodyne song so offensive that she left the table.
reasons: Picking something mild enough that nobody will complain matches the word's meaning.
Music meant to shock and rattle people is provocative, not bland.
This treats the word as if it meant old or antique; it has nothing to do with age.
Something truly inoffensive would not drive a listener away in protest.
